newsitem.title: GERMANY: German miners in mass protest over subsidies.
newsitem.headline: German miners in mass protest over subsidies.

text.p: About 100,000 miners and their supporters formed a 100-km (60-mile) human chain across Germany's industrial Ruhr heartland on Friday to protest against government plans to reduce coal subsidies.
The chain, linking the western cities of Dortmund, Duisburg and Essen, was organised by miners' union IG Bergbau.
It was sparked after Finance Minister Theo Waigel proposed the cuts under pressure to trim the budget to qualify for European monetary union (EMU),

Miners' leaders rejected the proposals to slash annual coal subsidies from their current level of 10 billion marks ($5.9 billion). IG Berbau leader Hans Berger said the industry needed at least 6.5 billion marks in annual support to stay afloat.
Some members of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) want to cut subsidies to 3.5 billion marks and eventually phase them out entirely.
"This is not enough to prevent disruption (in the industry) and not enough to achieve a socially acceptable transition," Berger told German radio in response to the proposals.
Berger said he hoped union leaders could meet government officials this month to reach a solution.

The bitter division within Kohl's ruling coalition over the issue was underscored by the presence of Labour Minister Norbert Bluem, often regarded as the government's social conscience, at the protest in solidarity with miners.
Kohl's office said the coalition, which has in the past been brought to the brink of collapse over coal subsidies, was standing firm and that cuts were inevitable.

"I see no way around it," Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl told journalists. "But it must be done in a socially acceptable way. We must keep the regional political situation in mind, and the labour market, and social concerns."

"But the miners can be sure the government, particularly the chancellor, will try to find a solution that will make possible, and guarantee, a viable mining industry for the future, but also a solution that's economically justifiable."
Bohl said no figures had been set yet and a decision was expected at the end of this month or the beginning of March.

The FDP, which views subsidies as being at odds with its market-based economic policies, warned the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) and ecological Greens who also joined the protest not to give the miners false hopes.

"It is in the interests of the workers to be honest and not to make promises that cannot be fulfilled," FDP general secretary Guido Westerwelle said in a statement, adding that each job in the industry costs the state 130,000 marks a year.

"These people must be given a chance to build their future once there is no more coal industry. Politicians should not limit their support to solidarity, but tackle the social and regional requirements for structural change," he said.
Coal miners wearing helmets lined the streets across the whole mining region holding burning torches and banners with slogans such as: "If the pit dies, the town dies too".
They were joined by members of other trade unions, German premier division football stars, church groups and whole schools of children with their teachers.
Current law commits Bonn to pay about 7.0 billion marks and state governments to pay 3.0 billion marks more in coal subsidies annually up to the year 2000.

Any move that would cut jobs is politically sensitive, given Germany's record unemployment levels. And the SPD, which governs the main coal-mining states of Saarland and North Rhine-Westphalia, looks set to keep the coal fires burning ahead of the 1998 elections.
Domestic hard coal, which must be mined from deep beneath the earth, costs several times as much as imports, but Bonn has deemed it right to maintain at least a token domestic industry.
The industry employs about 100,000 coal miners, down from about 600,000 in its 1950s heyday.
($ = 1.684 German Marks)
